# Overview

In Lab 5, you revised your Tucson bicycle accident visualization using more advanced `ggplot2` tools to create a polished visualization.
In this lab, you will take that same visualization and make it dynamic using Shiny.
Rather than creating a completely new analysis, you will build on the work you already completed.
The goal is to learn how Shiny can turn a static visualization into an interactive dashboard that responds to user input.

Before you begin, view the completed example app here: [Lab 6 Tucson Bicycle Accident Dashboard](https://jacobtnyoung.shinyapps.io/lab-06-plot/). 
Your goal is to recreate this dashboard on your own.
Your dashboard will allow users to select whether they want to view bicycle incidents that involved an injury, bicycle incidents that did not involve an injury, or both.
When the user changes the checkbox selection, the plot should update automatically.

This lab is designed to help you understand the basic structure of a Shiny application: 

  - the setup loads the packages and prepares the data
  - the user interface controls what the user sees and clicks
  - the server controls how the app responds to the user's choices
  - the output displays the updated visualization

## Part 1: Building the App

For this lab, you will begin with a partially completed Shiny app template. 
Download the [template for this lab](../labs/templates/lab-06-LastName.R) prior to beginning the lab. 
This file already contains the basic structure of the dashboard. 
Some pieces of the code have been removed. Your task is to complete the missing sections so the app recreates the [Lab 6 Tucson Bicycle Accident Dashboard](https://jacobtnyoung.shinyapps.io/lab-06-plot/).
You do not need to create a new RStudio project for this lab.
You can complete the assignment directly in the template file.
When you are ready to test the app, click **Run App** in RStudio.

## Analytical Briefing

## Analytical Briefing

In your briefing, explain how your Shiny dashboard works and how it builds on the visualization work you completed in Lab 5.

Your goal is to show that you understand how the different parts of the app work together. Do not simply describe what the final plot looks like. Instead, explain how the app uses data preparation, user input, filtering, summarizing, and plotting to create an interactive visualization.

Here are some things you should discuss:

  - Describe the purpose of the dashboard. What does the app allow a user to explore?
  - Explain how the app builds on the bicycle incident visualization from Lab 5.
  - Describe the role of the `ui` section. What does the user see and interact with?
  - Explain what the `checkboxGroupInput()` does.
  - Explain why the checkbox choices are `"No Injury"` and `"Injury"`.
  - Describe the role of the `server` section. What does the server do after the user makes a selection?
  - Explain how the `input$` is used to filter the data.
  - Describe how the app groups and summarizes the filtered data by `year` and `month`.
  - Explain how the summarized data are sent into `ggplot()`.
  - Discuss how the plot changes when the user selects only `"Injury"`, only `"No Injury"`, or both options.
  - Identify one additional feature you might add in the future if you wanted to make the app more useful.

### Expectations

Your briefing should demonstrate that you understand the basic Shiny workflow:

  - the `ui` creates the input and output spaces
  - the user makes a selection
  - the `server` uses that selection to filter the data
  - the filtered data are summarized
  - `renderPlot()` redraws the plot
  - the updated plot appears in the app

Focus on explaining the logic of the app in your own words. 
For example, instead of saying “I used `checkboxGroupInput()`,” explain that the checkbox lets the user choose which injury categories should be included in the plot. 
Similarly, instead of saying “I used `renderPlot()`,” explain that `renderPlot()` tells Shiny to redraw the visualization whenever the selected injury categories change.
Your briefing should make clear that the app is interactive because the user’s selection changes the data that are plotted.
